title: 02. Ingestion & Chunking: Document Loaders (PDF, DOCX, HTML, CSV, Web Scraping)
summary: Document loaders are the entry point of every RAG ingestion pipeline.

sections.title: ① Concept Explanation
sections.body: Document loaders are the entry point of every RAG ingestion pipeline. They convert raw, heterogeneous document formats — PDFs, Word documents, HTML pages, spreadsheets, and web content — into a normalized `Document` object containing raw text and metadata. The choice of loader profoundly impacts downstream quality: a naive PDF loader loses table structure, while a smarter one preserves it. In production, loaders must handle corrupt files, encoding errors, password-protected documents, and partial reads gracefully. LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Docling (2025) provide loader abstractions, but production systems often need custom parsers for proprietary formats.

diagrams.title: Ingestion pipeline with incremental updates
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  S["Sources — PDF, DOCX, HTML, CSV, web"] --> L["Loader"] --> P["Parse — text, tables, images"]
  P --> CL["Clean — headers, footers, boilerplate"] --> MD["Metadata — source, page, section, ACL, date"]
  MD --> CH["Chunk"] --> H{"content hash changed?"}
  H -- "no" --> SKIP["skip, keep old vector"]
  H -- "yes" --> EM["Embed"] --> IX[("Upsert to index")]
  IX --> DEL["Delete chunks no longer in the doc"]
diagrams.explain: Parsing quality decides retrieval quality. Keep **metadata** (source, page, section, permissions) on every chunk: you need it for citations and filtering. Hash each chunk so re-ingesting an unchanged document costs nothing, and delete chunks that disappeared so the index never cites outdated text.

sections.title: ④ Visual Explanation
sections.body:
```
DOCUMENT INGESTION PIPELINE
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

SOURCE DIVERSITY
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PDFs ──────┐
DOCX ──────┤
HTML ──────┤──▶ LOADER FACTORY ──▶ Document Objects
CSV  ──────┤       (routes to        {page_content: "...",
Web  ──────┘    appropriate loader)   metadata: {...}}
Scanned──┘

LOADER SELECTION DECISION TREE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Is it a PDF?
  ├─ Scanned (image-based)?  ──▶ Tesseract OCR (pytesseract)
  ├─ Text-based, simple?     ──▶ PyPDF (fast)
  ├─ Text-based, complex?    ──▶ Unstructured (hi_res mode)
  └─ Scientific/financial?   ──▶ Docling (vision transformer)

Is it DOCX?
  ├─ With tables?            ──▶ python-docx + table extractor
  └─ Text-only?              ──▶ UnstructuredWordDocumentLoader

Is it HTML?
  ├─ Static page?            ──▶ AsyncHtmlLoader + Html2Text
  └─ JS-rendered?            ──▶ Playwright + BeautifulSoup

Is it CSV/Excel?
  └─ Always                  ──▶ Pandas row-to-Document conversion

PRODUCTION SCALE ARCHITECTURE (10M PDFs)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    S3 Bucket (10M PDFs)
         │
         ▼
    SQS Queue (buffered messages)
         │
    ┌────┼────┐
    ▼    ▼    ▼   ... 32-1000 parallel workers
  W-1  W-2  W-3
   │    │    │
   └────┼────┘
         │  Each worker:
         │  download → parse → chunk → embed → upsert
         ▼
    Qdrant Cluster (sharded)

THROUGHPUT:
  32 workers × 2 PDF/sec = 64 PDF/sec
  10M / 64 = ~43 hours

  1000 Lambda × 2 PDF/sec = 2000 PDF/sec
  10M / 2000 = ~1.4 hours

INCREMENTAL UPDATE FLOW
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
New Document Version Uploaded
         │
         ▼
    Hash(content) == stored hash?
         │
    YES ─┘──▶ Skip (no change)
         │
    NO ──▶ Delete old vectors by doc_id filter
         │
         ▼
    Chunk → Embed → Upsert new vectors
         │
         ▼
    Update metadata (version, updated_at, new_hash)
```

quiz.question: What are the key differences between PyPDF, PDFMiner, and Unstructured for PDF loading?
options: Minimum required metadata for production RAG: source: file path or URL; doc_id: unique identifier for the document; chunk_id: unique identifier for this specific chunk.
Web scraping pitfalls: JavaScript-rendered content (requires Playwright/Selenium), dynamic pagination, rate limiting, robot.txt compliance, HTML noise (nav, ads,…
Scenario Q3-Q10: (Scanned PDFs with poor OCR quality, multilingual ingestion, ingestion pipeline failure recovery, handling 1GB PDFs, deduplication at scale,…

PyPDF2/PyPDF: Simple, fast, but loses table structure and formatting. Good for text-heavy PDFs with no tables; PDFMiner: Layout-aware text extraction, preserves column order better. Slower but more accurate for multi-column docs; Unstructured: Uses computer vision + heuristics to detect document elements (titles, paragraphs, tables, headers). Best for complex PDFs.….
quiz.explanation: PyPDF2/PyPDF: Simple, fast, but loses table structure and formatting. Good for text-heavy PDFs with no tables. PDFMiner: Layout-aware text extraction, preserves column order better.

quiz.question: How do you load and process DOCX files preserving heading structure?
options: Scenario Q3-Q10: (Scanned PDFs with poor OCR quality, multilingual ingestion, ingestion pipeline failure recovery, handling 1GB PDFs, deduplication at scale,…
Minimum required metadata for production RAG: source: file path or URL; doc_id: unique identifier for the document; chunk_id: unique identifier for this specific chunk.
Root Cause: Sequential processing is too slow — at 1 sec/PDF, 10M PDFs = 115 days.
DOCX files have rich structure (headings, styles, tables). Use python-docx directly or UnstructuredWordDocumentLoader to preserve hierarchy.
quiz.explanation: DOCX files have rich structure (headings, styles, tables). Use python-docx directly or UnstructuredWordDocumentLoader to preserve hierarchy. ---

options: Minimum required metadata for production RAG: source: file path or URL; doc_id: unique identifier for the document; chunk_id: unique identifier for this specific chunk.

CSV/Excel data needs special handling because rows represent discrete records.
quiz.explanation: CSV/Excel data needs special handling because rows represent discrete records. Don't chunk CSVs like text — instead, convert each row (or group of related rows) into a natural language document or JSON string. ---
